blocks.html:
Canada’s healthcare system stands at a critical juncture in 2026. 

With approximately 2.1 million healthcare workers forming the second-largest employment sector in the Canadian economy, the workforce faces unprecedented challenges balancing supply against surging demand. 

This comprehensive data hub synthesizes the most current statistics, trends, and projections shaping Canada’s healthcare workforce landscape.

Key Findings:

  • 5.7 million Canadian adults lack a regular healthcare provider (2024)
  • 49% increase in family physicians required to meet current demand
  • 78,600 job vacancies in health occupations (Q3 2024), with 48.5% open for 90+ days
  • Healthcare employment grew 8.4% between Q4 2019 and Q4 2023, adding 121,100 positions
  • Vacancy rates tripled from 2.1% (2016) to 5.8% (2024) in health-related occupations

1. Overall Healthcare Workforce Statistics

1.1 Total Employment in Healthcare

Historical Growth Trajectory (2004-2025):

  • 2004: 761,100 workers (6.1% of workforce)
  • 2016: 1,267,800 workers (7.4% of workforce)
  • 2024: 1,339,900 workers (7.8% of workforce)
  • 2025 (Year-End): 1,424,900 workers (8.3% of workforce)
  • 22-Year Growth: +663,800 workers (+87.2%)
  • Average Annual Growth Rate: 3.1% (vs. 1.6% across all occupations)

1.2 Workforce Composition by Sector (2026 updated)

Workforce Demographics:

  • Gender: 79% female, 21% male
  • Employment Status: 80% full-time, 20% part-time
  • Education Level: Characterized by high levels of post-secondary education
  • Average Age: Varies by profession (details below)

2. Physicians

2.1 National Physician Statistics (2026)

2.2 Family Physicians – Critical Shortage

Trends Over Time:

Per 10,000 Population (Supply Strategy)

  • 2019: 11.8
  • 2024: 11.5
  • 2026 (Projected): 11.4
  • Change: -3.4% (Declining as population growth from immigration continues to outpace new physician entries).

Direct Care Workforce (Frontline Impact)

  • 2023: 11.6 per 10,000 population
  • 2024: 11.5 per 10,000 population
  • 2025 (Latest): 11.4 per 10,000 population
  • Change: -1.7% over the last 24 months.

Growth Rate Deceleration (Long-term Pipeline)

  • 2012-2016: 12.9%
  • 2017-2021: 7.7%
  • 2022-2026: ~6.8% (Estimated)
  • Deceleration: -6.1 percentage points from the 2012 peak.

Practice Pattern Changes (Access Realities)

  • Average patients per family physician per year:
    • 2013: 1,746 patients
    • 2021: 1,353 patients
    • 2026 (Latest Study): ~1,280 patients
    • Change: -26.7% (Driven by “team-based care” models and higher administrative time).
  • Physician Diversion: Over 32% of family physicians now provide services primarily outside of traditional comprehensive primary care (up from 30%).
    • Emergency Medicine: 14.5%
    • Psychiatry/Mental Health: 5.4%
    • Sports Medicine/Sub-Specialties: 3.1%

Practice Pattern Changes:

  • Average patients per family physician per year:
    • 2013: 1,746 patients
    • 2021: 1,353 patients
    • Change: -22.5%
  • 30% of family physicians now provide services primarily outside primary care:
    • Emergency medicine: 14.2%
    • Psychiatry: 5.0%
    • General surgery: 2.1%

2.3 Physician Demographics

2.4 Physician Compensation (2023-2024)

Total Gross Clinical Payments:

  • 2022-2023: $32.5 billion
  • 2023-2024: $34.6 billion
  • Growth: +6.5%

3. Nursing Workforce

3.1 National Nursing Statistics (2024)

3.2 Nurse Practitioners – Fastest Growing Profession

Growth Trajectory:

  • 2020: 1.6 per 10,000 population
  • 2024: 2.2 per 10,000 population
  • 10-Year Average Annual Growth: 9% (highest among all health professions)

Direct Care Employment:

  • 2023: 6,826 NPs
  • 2024: 7,477 NPs
  • Growth: +651 (+9.5%)

Internationally Educated:

  • 2023: 4.6%
  • 2024: 4.5%

Supply-Demand Projections:

  • Expected to meet demand by 2031 if current training seat increases continue
  • Represents opportunity for workforce planners to expand NP roles in primary care

3.3 Registered Nurses – Backbone of Healthcare

Growth Patterns:

  • Comprise approximately 8 RNs per 1,000 population (largest health professional segment)
  • Recent growth slowdown:
    • 2021: 2.5% annual growth
    • 2022: 1.1% annual growth
    • Deceleration: -1.4 percentage points

Direct Care Trends:

  • Hospital RN direct care workforce declined 0.6% (2021-2022)
  • Long-term care: 2,500 fewer nurses (-5.1%) working directly with patients (2021-2022)

Age Distribution Concerns:

  • Number of RNs aged 45-64 has decreased substantially
  • More RNs leaving direct care earlier in their careers

3.4 Internationally Educated Nurses (IENs)

Contribution to Workforce:

  • 2017: 8% of newly licensed nurses
  • 2022: 12% of newly licensed nurses
  • Growth: +4 percentage points

Recent Immigration Patterns:

  • In 2021, recent immigrants (13.0%) and non-permanent residents (10.8%) together accounted for 23.8% of all nurse aides, orderlies, and patient service associates aged 25-34

4. Allied Health Professionals

4.1 Comprehensive Supply Statistics (2023)

4.2 Fastest Growing and Declining Professions (2022-2023)

Fastest Growing:

  1. Psychotherapists/Counselling Therapists: +16.3%
  2. Nurse Practitioners: +9.7%
  3. Physiotherapists: +4.0%
  4. Occupational Therapists: +3.0%
  5. Licensed Practical Nurses: +3.0%

Declining Professions:

  1. Environmental Public Health Professionals: -7.7%
  2. Medical Laboratory Technologists: -1.5%
  3. Dental Assistants: -1.4%

4.3 Pharmacists

Supply Statistics:

  • Total: ~50,000 pharmacists
  • Growth rate deceleration:
    • 2013-2017: 3.4% average annual growth
    • 2018-2022: 2.2% average annual growth

Internationally Educated:

  • More than one-third (>33%) of pharmacists are international graduates
  • Highest proportion among allied health professionals

Expanded Scope:

  • Increasing prescribing authority for minor ailments across provinces
  • Providing immunizations, medication reviews, chronic disease consultations
  • Integration into primary care teams

5. Personal Support Workers (PSWs)

5.1 National PSW Statistics

Current Workforce (2022):

  • Approximately 350,000 PSWs employed across all sectors
  • Expected to need 700,000+ by 2032 (more than doubling)

5.2 Provincial Data – Alberta (Most Detailed Available)

Note: Alberta data likely under-reported as enrollment in Health Care Aide Directory is mandatory only for public sector workers.

5.3 Projected Requirements by Sector (2022-2043)

5.4 Ontario-Specific Projections

Projected Shortages by Year:

  • 2032: 50,853 PSWs needed (government projections)
  • This represents a critical workforce gap requiring immediate attention

5.5 Compensation and Working Conditions

Hourly Wage Ranges (2024-2025):

  • National Average: $15.50 – $26.00 per hour
  • Ontario Urban Areas: $23.00 – $28.00 per hour
  • Entry Level (<1 year): $18.38 per hour
  • Early Career (1-4 years): $19.92 per hour
  • Maximum Pay: $25.16 per hour

Annual Salary Estimates:

  • Typical range: $40,000 – $50,000

Workforce Challenges:

  • 63% have left or seriously considered leaving jobs in past 2 years (2024 survey)
  • 70% experience monthly burnout
  • High turnover rates affecting continuity of care

6. Job Vacancies and Labour Demand

6.1 Overall Healthcare Vacancy Statistics

Key Trends:

  • Vacancy rates nearly tripled from 2016 to 2024
  • Despite recent declines, vacancies remain elevated compared to pre-pandemic (39,000 in Q4 2019)
  • Year-over-year decline Q1 2024 to Q1 2025: -17,600 (-19.1%)

6.2 Vacancies by Occupation (Q3 2024, Not Seasonally Adjusted)

Top 3 Occupations Account for:

  • 63% of all health occupation vacancies (Q1 2025)

6.3 Long-Duration Vacancies

90+ Days Open:

  • Overall Health Occupations: 48.5% of vacancies (Q3 2024)
  • Licensed Practical Nurses: 49.9%
  • Nursing & Allied Health Professionals: 52.5%
  • Professional Health Occupations: 53.9%
  • National Average (All Occupations): 31.6%

Comparison:

  • Health occupations have the highest proportion of long-duration vacancies among 10 broad occupational categories

6.4 Regional Vacancy Disparities (2024)

Key Findings:

  • Remote regions have vacancy rates nearly twice as high as accessible regions (9.3% vs. 5.5%)
  • Despite higher offered wages, remote vacancies remain open longer
  • Challenges in remote areas cannot be explained by wages alone

LPN Vacancy Rates by Region:

  • Accessible: 12.0%
  • Remote: 24.5% (more than double)

PSW Offered Wages (Inverse Pattern):

  • Accessible: $23.91/hour
  • Remote: $22.63/hour (lower in remote areas)

7. Supply-Demand Projections (2022-2034)

7.1 Projected Gaps by Profession (Base Case Scenario)

7.2 Key Projection Insights

Worsening Gaps:

  • Family physicians, RNs, and pharmacists face growing shortages
  • Gap between supply and demand expected to widen significantly

Improving Situations:

  • NP supply projected to meet demand by 2031 (with continued training seat increases)
  • LPNs, RPNs, occupational therapists, and physiotherapists showing positive trajectories

Critical Note:

  • Even professions showing improvement are starting from significant existing shortages
  • Population growth and aging demographics create continuously moving targets

8. Internationally Educated Health Professionals (IEHPs)

8.1 National Statistics (2021 Census)

Total IEHPs in Canada:

  • 259,695 internationally educated health care professionals (ages 18-64)
  • Represent 13% of all Canadians with postsecondary health education
  • Nearly 1/3 (31%) arrived in Canada between 2016-2021

8.2 Distribution by Province

8.3 Labour Market Outcomes

Employment Rates:

  • IEHPs: 76%
  • Canadian-educated health professionals: 80%
  • Gap: -4 percentage points

Working in Health Occupations:

  • Overall: 58% of employed IEHPs work in health occupations
  • By field of study:
    • Nursing: 69%
    • Medicine: 67%
    • Pharmacy: 63%
    • Dentistry: 60%

Best Performing Provinces (% IEHPs in Health Occupations):

  1. Newfoundland & Labrador: 74%
  2. Nova Scotia: 65%+
  3. Saskatchewan: 65%+
  4. Rest of Canada: 46%

8.4 Educational Profile

Highest Level of Education:

  • Bachelor’s degree: 35%
  • Medical/Dental/Optometry degree: 20%
  • Below bachelor’s degree: 25%
  • Graduate degrees: 20%

Region of Education:

  • Asia: 63%
  • English-speaking Western countries: 11%
  • French-speaking European countries: 4%
  • Other: 22%

8.5 Immigration and Credential Recognition Initiatives

Federal Investments (2024-2026):

  • $77.1 million over 4 years for IEHP integration
    • 120 specific training positions
    • Increased assessment capacity
    • Support for credential recognition navigation
  • $86 million to 15 organizations for foreign credential recognition
    • Target: 6,600 IEHPs

Practice Eligibility Routes:

  • $1.49 million to expand Practice Eligibility Route for International Medical Graduates
  • $500,000 to understand barriers in existing programs

Provincial Initiatives:

  • British Columbia: Practice Ready Assessment expanded from 32 to 96 seats (tripled)
  • Ontario: Prohibiting Canadian work experience requirements (with exceptions)
  • Multiple provinces: Streamlined licensing, zero-cost registration pathways, bridging programs.

9. Workforce Renewal and Demographics

9.1 Age Distribution Challenges

Renewal Ratio (2024):

  • 1.9 younger workers (ages 25-34) for every worker aged 55-64 in health occupations
  • Signals workforce renewal pressure

Physicians Nearing Retirement:

  • 500,000 healthcare workers over age 55 (expected retirements within next decade)

Working Age Population Near Retirement (2021):

  • Record high 21.8% of working-aged population was 55-64 years old
  • Puts downward pressure on labour supply across all sectors

9.2 Immigration as Workforce Renewal Source

Nurse Aides, Orderlies, and Patient Service Associates (Ages 25-34, 2021):

  • Recent immigrants: 13.0%
  • Non-permanent residents: 10.8%
  • Combined: 23.8% of workforce in this age group

Education Levels of Immigrant PSWs:

  • 47.1% of recent immigrant PSWs have bachelor’s degree or higher
  • Only 6.3% of Canadian-born PSWs have bachelor’s degree or higher
  • Indicates significant credential underutilization

9.3 Gender Distribution

Overall Healthcare Workforce:

  • Female: 79%
  • Male: 21%

By Profession:

10. Hospital Staffing and Agency Use

10.1 Hospital Workforce Indicators

Overtime Trends:

  • Steady rise in overtime hours (paid and unpaid) since pandemic
  • Critical for understanding true physician and nurse workload capacity

Direct Care Workforce Changes:

  • RNs in hospital direct care: -0.6% (2021-2022)
  • Long-term care nurses: -2,500 positions (-5.1%) (2021-2022)

10.2 Private Staffing Agency Usage

National Statistics (2023-2024):

  • Total Agency Hours: 7.8 million hours
  • Full-Time Equivalent: 4,010 FTE
  • % of All Worked Hours: 1%

Rural and Remote Hospitals:

  • Agency Hours: 2.1 million hours
  • Full-Time Equivalent: 1,090 FTE
  • % of All Worked Hours: >3%
  • Growth Since 2019-2020: +250%

Cost Implications:

  • Agency hours are more costly than regular staffing
  • May not be sustainable long-term
  • Indicates severe recruitment and retention challenges

11. Education and Training Capacity

11.1 Medical Education

Undergraduate Medical Education (UGME) Seats:

  • Gradual expansion across provinces
  • Ontario: Adding 100 new undergraduate seats
  • British Columbia: Expansion of up to 40 UGME seats (complete by 2024)
  • Simon Fraser University: First entirely new medical school in Western Canada in 55 years

Postgraduate Medical Training:

  • Ontario: Adding 154 postgraduate positions over 3 years
  • British Columbia: 122 new residences by 2028

Residency Matching Trends:

  • Unfilled family medicine residency seats decreased by almost 15 percentage points over past decade
  • Largely due to recruitment of international medical graduates in second-round matching

International Medical Graduate (IMG) Positions:

  • Increased allocation of residency positions for IMGs
  • Second-round matching has become critical for filling family medicine spots

11.2 Medical Residents – Training Location (2024-2025)

Family Medicine Residency:

  • Higher proportion of IMGs compared to other specialties
  • Critical for addressing family physician shortage

11.3 Nursing Education Challenges

Barriers to Expansion:

  • Shortage of faculty members and preceptors
  • Limited clinical placements
  • Healthcare settings strained to accommodate students
  • Results in attrition from programs and failure to retain newly licensed nurses

Solutions Required:

  • Work environment improvements for retention
  • Investment in simulated learning opportunities
  • Adequate remuneration/incentives for preceptors
  • Increased administrative resources and funding

NP Education:

  • Training seats increasing
  • Expected to meet demand by 2031 with current trajectory

11.4 Allied Health Education

Occupational Therapy and Physiotherapy Specific Challenges:

  • Excessive patient contact hour requirements for accreditation
  • Significant barrier to accepting more students
  • Difficulty accommodating learners when healthcare delivery is strained

General Challenges Across Professions:

  • Limited number of teachers, faculty, preceptors
  • Scarcity of clinical placements
  • Insufficient administrative resources
  • Lack of investment in simulated learning

11.5 PSW Training Trends (2018-2023)

Applications:

  • Most community colleges reported no change or decrease
  • Some programs showing increased applications
  • Overall positive trend but not widespread enough

Enrolment:

  • Over 1/3 of training programs reported fewer students since pandemic
  • Despite millions in government investment

Completions:

  • Mixed results across institutions
  • More programs reporting increases than decreases
  • But insufficient to meet projected demand

Government Investments:

  • Ontario: Free tuition and workforce-entry bonuses
  • Alberta: HCA Education Bursary Program ($9,000 per student)
  • Federal: National occupational standard for personal care providers

12. Retention and Burnout

12.1 Reasons for Leaving Healthcare Jobs

Top Factors Cited:

  • Workplace burnout
  • High patient workloads
  • Administrative burden
  • Fear for personal safety
  • Inadequate compensation
  • Limited career advancement opportunities
  • Poor work-life balance

12.2 Burnout Statistics by Profession

Physicians:

  • Unprecedented levels of burnout reported in 2021 National Physician Health Survey
  • Particularly acute among:
    • Cancer care physicians in Ontario
    • Cardiovascular physicians

Nurses:

  • CFNU Member Survey (2024) documented high burnout rates
  • Long-term care nurses especially affected during and post-pandemic
  • Workplace-related distress contributing to exits

Pharmacists:

  • National survey shows mental health has improved but continued challenges
  • Need for more support and investments

Personal Support Workers:

  • 63% have left or seriously considered leaving in past 2 years (2024)
  • 70% experience monthly burnout
  • Highest turnover rates in healthcare workforce

12.3 Retention Initiatives

National:

  • $3.5 million to RCPSC for National Plan for Health Workforce Well-Being
  • Nursing Retention Toolkit developed with nursing community
  • Criminal Code amendments to protect health workers from threats/violence
  • $100 million for mental health support (COVID-affected workers)
  • $50 million for PTSD support (frontline workers)

Provincial Examples:

  • British Columbia: Peer support and mentoring programs ($99.5 million over 3 years for nursing)
  • Ontario: 11% wage increase for hospital nurses over 2 years (as of July 2023)
  • Multiple provinces: Retention bonuses, signing bonuses, return-of-service agreements

13. Scope of Practice Expansions

13.1 2024 Policy Changes

Nurse Practitioners:

  • Expanded prescribing authority across most jurisdictions
  • Broader scope for managing minor ailments independently
  • Some provinces adding prescribing powers for certain medications

Registered Nurses:

  • Newfoundland and Labrador: Prescribing powers with training
  • Ontario: Prescribing powers with training
  • British Columbia: Prescribing powers with training

Licensed Practical Nurses:

  • Ontario: Regulations allowing independent performance of certain controlled acts in specific settings

Pharmacists:

  • Most jurisdictions: Expanded prescribing for minor ailments
  • Growing role in immunizations and chronic disease management
  • Integration into primary care teams

Midwives:

  • Expanded prescribing powers in several provinces

Paramedics:

  • Some provinces allowing delivery of medical diagnostic services in community settings

13.2 Impact on Workforce Utilization

Benefits:

  • Better utilization of highly skilled professionals
  • Improved access to care, especially in underserved areas
  • Reduced burden on family physicians
  • Decreased wait times for specific services

Challenges:

  • Need for adequate training and support
  • Ensuring patient safety and quality of care
  • Coordination across professions
  • Resistance from some professional groups

14. Primary Care Access Crisis

14.1 Canadians Without Regular Healthcare Provider

2024 Statistics:

  • 5.7 million Canadian adults lack regular healthcare provider
  • Represents significant barrier to timely, preventive care

Children and Youth (2024):

  • 11% without primary care provider
  • Most commonly due to:
    • Waitlists
    • No clinics accepting new patients

Access Gaps:

  • 89% of children/youth have primary care provider
  • 11% gap represents hundreds of thousands without access

14.2 Nurses Serving Seniors

Metric Deterioration:

  • 2013: 59 nurses per 1,000 seniors (age 65+)
  • 2022: 52 nurses per 1,000 seniors
  • Decline: -11.9%

Implications:

  • Supply not keeping pace with aging population
  • Increased workload per nurse caring for seniors
  • Quality of care concerns

15. Provincial and Territorial Spotlight

15.1 Ontario

Healthcare Employment (2023):

  • 971,100 workers (12.3% of provincial workforce)
  • GDP Contribution: $62.4 billion (2024)

Key Initiatives:

  • 100 new undergraduate medical education seats
  • 154 new postgraduate positions over 3 years
  • Prohibiting Canadian work experience requirements for licensing (with exceptions)
  • 11% wage increase for hospital nurses over 2 years (July 2023)

Physician Statistics (2024):

  • 45,932 active physicians
  • Physician-to-population ratio: 104.7 per 100,000

PSW Projections:

  • 50,853 additional PSWs needed by 2032

15.2 British Columbia

Key Investments and Initiatives:

  • Practice Ready Assessment seats tripled from 32 to 96
  • 40 new UGME seats (completed 2024)
  • 122 new residency positions by 2028
  • $99.5 million over 3 years for nursing recruitment and retention
  • Simon Fraser University Medical School (first new medical school in Western Canada in 55 years)

IEHP Population:

  • 45,235 internationally educated healthcare professionals

15.3 Alberta

Personal Support Workers:

  • 28,525 PSWs in 2024 (down from 29,516 in 2020)
  • 58.3 per 10,000 population
  • 60% employed part-time or casual

Education Investments:

  • HCA Education Bursary Program: $9,000 per student

IEHP Population:

  • 42,035 internationally educated healthcare professionals (68% educated in Asia)

15.4 Quebec

Healthcare Workforce:

  • Unique regulatory landscape with professional orders
  • IEHP population: 30,595 (55% educated in Asia)
  • French language requirements add complexity to IEHP integration

15.5 Prairie Provinces

Manitoba:

  • 11,680 IEHPs (75% educated in Asia)
  • High reliance on internationally educated professionals

Saskatchewan:

  • 7,280 IEHPs (73% educated in Asia)
  • 65%+ of IEHPs working in health occupations (among highest in Canada)

15.6 Atlantic Provinces

Nova Scotia:

  • 3,195 IEHPs (58% educated in Asia)
  • 65%+ of IEHPs working in health occupations (among highest in Canada)

New Brunswick:

  • 1,675 IEHPs
  • Unique pattern: 21% educated in English-speaking Western countries (highest proportion nationally)

Newfoundland & Labrador:

  • 915 IEHPs (65% educated in Asia)
  • Highest IEHP utilization rate in Canada: 74% working in health occupations
  • RN prescribing powers with training

Prince Edward Island:

  • 475 IEHPs (60% educated in Asia)
  • Small population requires targeted recruitment strategies

16. Geographic Distribution and Rural Challenges

16.1 Urban vs. Rural Physician Distribution

All Physicians:

  • Urban locations: 93%
  • Rural locations: 7%
  • Population distribution disparity not adequately addressed

Family Physicians:

  • Rural areas particularly underserved
  • Higher proportion of older physicians in rural settings
  • Recruitment and retention challenges

16.2 Rural Health Workforce Challenges

Vacancy Rates (2024):

  • Remote: 9.3%
  • Less Accessible: 7.2%
  • Accessible: 5.5%

Remote Regions:

  • Vacancy rates nearly double accessible regions
  • Remain open longer despite higher offered wages
  • Non-wage factors critical (housing, family considerations, professional isolation)

LPN Vacancies:

  • Remote: 24.5%
  • Accessible: 12.0%
  • More than double in remote areas

16.3 Northern and Remote Communities

Unique Challenges:

  • Limited infrastructure
  • Geographic isolation
  • Cultural competency requirements
  • High turnover rates
  • Reliance on temporary staffing solutions

Agency Use in Rural/Remote Hospitals:

  • 2.1 million agency hours (2023-2024)
  • Represents >3% of all worked hours
  • 250% increase since 2019-2020

17. Technology and Workforce Transformation

17.1 Virtual Care Adoption

Post-Pandemic Permanence:

  • Telehealth and virtual care permanently expanded healthcare delivery options
  • Some provinces reporting 30-40% of primary care visits conducted virtually

Impact on Workforce:

  • Allows physicians to serve larger geographic areas
  • Enables consultations across provincial boundaries (with regulatory cooperation)
  • Reduces travel burden for patients and providers
  • Questions remain about equitable access and appropriate use

17.2 Digital Health Tools

Adoption Areas:

  • Electronic medical records (EMRs)
  • E-prescribing
  • Remote patient monitoring
  • AI-assisted diagnostics (emerging)

Workforce Implications:

  • Training requirements for digital literacy
  • Time savings in documentation and coordination
  • Cybersecurity and privacy considerations
  • Variable adoption rates across provinces and practice settings

17.3 Automation and AI

Potential Applications:

  • Administrative task automation
  • Diagnostic support
  • Medication management
  • Workflow optimization

Current Status (2024-2026):

  • Early adoption phase
  • Limited large-scale implementation
  • Regulatory frameworks under development
  • Workforce skill requirements evolving

18. Compensation Trends and Economics

18.1 Physician Compensation Growth (2023-2024)

Total Clinical Payments:

  • 2022-2023: $32.5 billion
  • 2023-2024: $34.6 billion
  • Growth: +6.5%

Average Gross Clinical Payments by Specialty (2023-2024):

  • All Physicians: $383,000
  • Family Medicine: $324,000
  • Medical Specialists: $406,000
  • Surgical Specialists: $556,000

Payment Model Distribution:

  • Fee-for-service: 72%
  • Alternative payment arrangements: 28%

18.2 Nurse Compensation

Registered Nurses (2024 Estimates):

  • Entry level: $55,000 – $65,000
  • Mid-career: $70,000 – $85,000
  • Senior/Specialized: $85,000 – $105,000

Nurse Practitioners:

  • Average: $95,000 – $115,000
  • Range varies significantly by province and practice setting

Licensed Practical Nurses:

  • Average: $48,000 – $62,000

Recent Adjustments:

  • Ontario hospital nurses: 11% increase over 2 years (July 2023)
  • Various provinces offering recruitment bonuses ($5,000-$20,000)
  • Retention bonuses in hard-to-recruit areas

18.3 Allied Health Compensation

Pharmacists:

  • Average: $95,000 – $110,000
  • Community pharmacy often lower than hospital/clinical

Physiotherapists:

  • Average: $65,000 – $85,000
  • Private practice highly variable

Occupational Therapists:

  • Average: $65,000 – $80,000

18.4 Personal Support Workers

Hourly Wages (2024-2025):

  • National average: $15.50 – $26.00
  • Ontario urban: $23.00 – $28.00
  • Entry level: $18.38
  • Early career (1-4 years): $19.92
  • Maximum: $25.16

Annual Salaries:

  • Typical: $40,000 – $50,000
  • Full-time equivalents often difficult to achieve due to part-time/casual nature

Regional Variations:

  • Remote offered wages (PSW): $22.63 (lower than accessible regions)
  • Accessible: $23.91

Compensation Challenges:

  • Wages not commensurate with demanding nature of work
  • Benefits often limited for part-time/casual workers
  • Contributing factor to high turnover and recruitment difficulties

19. Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion

19.1 Gender Representation

Overall Healthcare Workforce:

  • 79% female, 21% male
  • Significant gender imbalance in most health professions

Physician Gender Trends:

  • New graduates: Majority female
  • Medical specialists: 43% female
  • Surgical specialists: 35% female (lowest)
  • Family physicians: 51% female (parity achieved)

Future Outlook:

  • Expected shift toward female-majority physician workforce
  • Implications for part-time work preferences and work-life balance considerations

19.2 Indigenous Health Workforce

Current Status (Limited Data Available):

  • Significant underrepresentation relative to population
  • Growing emphasis on cultural competency training
  • Indigenous-led health services requiring Indigenous healthcare providers

Initiatives:

  • Targeted recruitment programs at medical and nursing schools
  • Indigenous health curricula development
  • Support for Indigenous students in health professions

19.3 Racial and Ethnic Diversity

Internationally Educated Professionals:

  • 63% of IEHPs educated in Asia
  • Significant contributions to workforce diversity
  • Underutilization of credentials remains concern

Cultural Competency:

  • Increasing emphasis in education and practice
  • Language diversity in healthcare delivery
  • Need for diverse workforce to serve diverse population

22. Methodology and Data Limitations

Data Collection Approach:

This data hub aggregates the most recent publicly available statistics from multiple authoritative sources, with priority given to:

  1. Government statistical agencies (CIHI, Statistics Canada)
  2. Professional regulatory bodies and associations
  3. Peer-reviewed research and official reports
  4. Provincial health ministries and authorities

Temporal Coverage:

  • Primary focus: 2024-2026 data
  • Historical comparisons: 2016-2024
  • Projections: Up to 2043 where available

Known Limitations:

Data Lag:

  • Most comprehensive national data has 1-2 year lag
  • Some statistics represent 2023-2024 figures reported in 2025-2026

Definitional Variations:

  • Different provinces may define occupational categories differently
  • “Direct care” vs. “total workforce” distinctions vary
  • Part-time equivalent calculations not standardized

Coverage Gaps:

  • PSW data particularly challenging (not universally regulated)
  • Private sector employment often under-reported
  • Rural and remote data less comprehensive
  • Some professions lack national coordination

Projection Uncertainty:

  • Supply-demand models rely on assumptions about immigration, education capacity, retention rates
  • Policy changes can rapidly alter projections
  • Pandemic effects create unusual baseline periods

Privacy and Confidentiality:

  • Small cell sizes suppressed in some regional data
  • Individual-level data aggregated, limiting granular analysis

Data Quality Ratings:

High Confidence (Robust National Datasets):

  • Physician supply and demographics
  • Registered nurse supply
  • Overall job vacancy rates
  • IEHP census data

Moderate Confidence (Some Gaps or Lags):

  • Allied health professional supply
  • Nurse practitioner growth rates
  • Provincial workforce distributions
  • Compensation data

Lower Confidence (Limited Standardization):

  • Personal support worker statistics
  • Burnout and retention rates
  • Rural-specific detailed breakdowns
  • Future demand projections beyond 5 years

Conclusion

With 2.1 million dedicated professionals serving a growing and aging population, the system faces simultaneous challenges of supply shortages, geographic maldistribution, burnout and retention crises, and evolving care delivery models.

The data paint a clear picture: despite growth in absolute numbers, supply has not kept pace with demand across most health professions. 

The 49% shortage of family physicians, 78,600 persistent job vacancies, and projected need to more than double the PSW workforce by 2032 represent urgent policy imperatives.

Yet opportunities exist. Internationally educated health professionals represent 13% of the health-educated workforce and a critical recruitment pathway. 

Scope of practice expansions for nurses, pharmacists, and other professionals can improve access and efficiency. 

Technology and virtual care offer tools to extend workforce reach. Strategic investments in education, credential recognition, and retention can bend the curve.

The path forward requires coordinated action across federal, provincial, and territorial governments, educational institutions, professional organizations, employers, and individual health workers. 

The decisions made in 2026-2027 will shape healthcare delivery for decades to come.
